vocabulary.gloss: The register in which the dates of hearing of the cases before a court are entered. Volume III makes the presiding officer himself fix fresh dates in the peshi register when an unexpected holiday or absence wipes out a day's list, and then hand the register to the reader of the court, who is responsible for telling the parties and witnesses who turn up at a closed court what their new date is. It is the paper ancestor of the CIS cause list, and 'peshi' remains the everyday word for a date of appearance in a Haryana court.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-A.10

vocabulary.gloss: The direction that once the examination of witnesses has begun the proceedings continue from day to day until the witnesses in attendance have been examined, with reasons recorded in writing for any adjournment beyond the following day. Volume III repeats it twice, for speedy disposal generally and for the stage after the accusation is put. It is the local counterpart of s.143(3) of the NI Act, which asks that a cheque trial be concluded within six months of the filing of the complaint, and the standard against which the years a NACT case actually takes are measured.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-D.11

vocabulary.gloss: The lighter record a summons case and a summary trial get. In a summons case the record is ordinarily a memorandum of the substance of the evidence and no more; in a summary case in which no appeal lies no evidence need be recorded at all, only the prescribed particulars in the summary register, but where an appeal does lie the magistrate must record the substance of the evidence and the particulars, and write a judgment before passing sentence. Since a cheque case is tried summarily and carries an appeal, this is the shape of the trial record a s.138 file actually ends up with.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-E.8
aka: memorandum of the substance of the evidence

vocabulary.gloss: Dismissal of a complaint case because the complainant did not appear. Volume III opens the chapter with the warning that some magistrates are inclined to dismiss cases in default hastily, and then requires the magistrate to consider whether such an order is legal and whether it is justified by the circumstances, and to record his reasons in every case. A complainant absent when the case is first called must have it called again later, and the time of dismissal must be noted on the record. This is the check a dismissed cheque complaint is revived on, in revision.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-F.2
aka: dismissal for absence of the complainant

vocabulary.gloss: In a summons case instituted on a complaint, if the complainant fails to attend on a day fixed for hearing the accused is to be acquitted, unless the magistrate adjourns the hearing or dispenses with the complainant's attendance and proceeds. A s.138 case is tried as a summons case, so this is not a mere dismissal - the accused walks free on the merits, and the complainant's remedy is revision, not a fresh complaint. It is the procedural risk the complainant carries on every single date.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-D.5
aka: acquittal for non-appearance of the complainant

vocabulary.gloss: The Volume III rule that a fine, though the lightest punishment a criminal court can impose, must never be excessive with reference to the means of the offender. Indiscriminate fines only waste the time of the courts and the police in trying to realise them and harass the convict and his dependants. On a s.138 conviction the fine may run to twice the amount of the cheque, so this is the state-level counterweight a Haryana magistrate applies when fixing it, and the reason the sentence in default is set with the status of the accused in mind.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 19-B.1
aka: fine in proportion to the offender's means
capacity of the convict to pay

vocabulary.gloss: Imprisonment ordered to be served if the fine is not paid. Volume III confirms that criminal courts are empowered to impose it but only subject to the limits the penal code sets, and asks that it be regulated with regard to the status of the accused so that he is induced to pay rather than to evade payment. In a cheque case, where the fine can be twice the cheque amount, the default sentence is often the only thing that actually moves money.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 19-B.2
aka: imprisonment in default of payment of fine

vocabulary.gloss: Where an offender is sentenced to a fine and to imprisonment in default and does not pay at once, the court may order that the fine be paid within a stated period or by instalments. Volume III points the magistrate at the power expressly. In a s.138 case this is the ordinary route by which a convicted drawer pays the cheque amount over to the complainant without going to jail, and it is the sentencing side of the settlements that end most cheque cases.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 19-B.3
aka: postponement of realisation of the fine

vocabulary.gloss: The court's treasurer and custodian. The nazir holds cash and property in the court's keeping, and pays out the money side of a case: the memorandum of the costs of witnesses is made out and forwarded to him, and property sent in by the police is made over to him for custody. The office is the nazarat branch. In a cheque case the nazir is who a witness's diet and road money comes from, and where a fine or a deposit is lodged.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 9-A.3

vocabulary.gloss: The daily allowance, with road money, paid to a witness who attends a criminal court. Volume III sets out when the court pays these expenses and carries a whole set of State instructions written for the nazarat officers and the presiding officers to prevent fraud and embezzlement in their disbursement. In a cheque case they are what the bank official who proves the return memo is entitled to, and one of the practical reasons a bank witness is better examined over a live link.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 9-B.1

vocabulary.gloss: The officer who administers e-filing. Under the E-Filing Rules the Administrator is, for the High Court, the Registrar (IT) or an officer appointed by the Chief Justice, and for a district court the officer or official appointed by the District and Sessions Judge. Everything that has to be unlocked in an e-filed case goes through him, including transferring an action from a litigant in person to the advocate later engaged. This is the formal name for the office the Panchkula filing assistants call the computer room and telephone before an e-filed NACT case can be released into their queue.
vocabulary.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 3.2

vocabulary.gloss: The defined term that decides whether the e-filing regime reaches a cheque case at all. An Action under the E-Filing Rules includes all proceedings instituted in the court or tribunal, and criminal complaints are named expressly, alongside suits, petitions, appeals, revisions and interlocutory applications. So a s.138 complaint is inside the e-filing rules and not merely a civil-side facility, and every rule that follows - formatting, digital signature, court fees, retention of originals, computation of time - applies to it.
vocabulary.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 3.1

vocabulary.gloss: A counter at which a case can be filed electronically over the court's intranet instead of over the internet, together with the e-Service Centres provided for the purpose. The E-Filing Rules apply to both online e-filing and e-filing through designated counters, and filing at a counter is permitted up to 1600 hours on a court working day. For a filer who has no digital signature, or whose document will not scan, this is the staffed alternative to the portal - and the point at which the e-filing regime meets the physical filing window.
vocabulary.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 2

vocabulary.gloss: The date on which an action is treated as filed electronically: the date it is received in the Registry within the prescribed time on a working day, reckoned in Indian Standard Time. Online filing after midnight counts as the next day, and filing on a gazetted holiday or a day the court is closed counts as the next working day; failure of the portal is no ground for exemption from limitation. Limitation is otherwise the same regime as physical filing. This is what fixes whether a cheque complaint is inside the one month allowed by s.142(1)(b) of the NI Act.
vocabulary.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 15

vocabulary.gloss: The duty on a party who e-files scanned documents to keep the originals for production or inspection as the court directs, to preserve a signed vakalatnama or an attested affidavit for at least two years after final disposal including appeal, and to bear the burden of producing the originals and proving they are genuine. Some documents must be kept permanently - and a negotiable instrument is one of them, except a cheque. So the cheque, which is the whole of a s.138 case, sits under the ordinary rule and has to be produced when the court calls for it.
vocabulary.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 11

vocabulary.gloss: The form an e-filed document has to take. All original typed material must be prepared as the Rules and Orders require and converted into an optical-character-recognition searchable PDF, and documents that are not text - scans, photographs - must be scanned to the stated standard. It is the bar the cheque, the bank return memo and the demand notice have to clear before an e-filed cheque complaint will be accepted, and the reason the Panchkula assistants ask for a clean PDF copy of a physical file.
vocabulary.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 7

vocabulary.gloss: A live television link or other audio-video electronic arrangement by which a person who is physically absent from the courtroom is nevertheless virtually present in it, to give evidence and be cross-examined. The Video Conferencing Rules make video conferencing available at all stages of a judicial proceeding and treat a proceeding conducted that way as a judicial proceeding for every purpose, using the software the High Court designates. Chapter 1 Part BB of Volume III is what carries these Rules into the criminal courts where a cheque case is tried.
vocabulary.source: Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 2(ix)

vocabulary.gloss: The courtroom, or any place where the court is physically convened, in a hearing held over a live link - including the place where a commissioner or an inquiring officer holds proceedings on the court's directions. It is the anchor end of a video-conferenced hearing: the judge, the record and the coordinator who runs the link sit at the Court Point, and a document at the Court Point is shown to a remote witness by transmitting an image of it.
vocabulary.source: Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 2(v)

vocabulary.gloss: The place where a person appears or is examined through a video link. It may be another court, a legal services authority or mediation centre, a jail, a hospital, or an Indian consulate abroad, and the Rules name who acts as coordinator at each. A summons to a witness who is to be examined by video conferencing must state the date, time and venue of the Remote Point and direct him to attend there in person with proof of identity. In a cheque case this is usually where the out-of-station complainant or the bank official appears from.
vocabulary.source: Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 2(x)

vocabulary.gloss: The defined class of people who may take part in a hearing over a live link: the person to be examined, the person in whose presence proceedings are to be recorded, an advocate or a party in person who intends to examine a witness, anyone required to make submissions, and anyone else the court permits to appear by video conferencing. In a s.138 case it covers the complainant, the accused whose personal attendance has been dispensed with, and the bank witness.
vocabulary.source: Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 2(xii)

vocabulary.gloss: The official who runs a video-conferenced hearing at each end. There is a coordinator at the Court Point and, where a witness or an accused is to be examined, one at the Remote Point as well; in the district judiciary they are nominated by the High Court or the District Judge. Who it is depends on where the remote end sits - a consular official abroad, a nominated official of another district court, the jail superintendent, a medical superintendent, or an officer of the legal services authority. The coordinator identifies the person appearing, and identifies and accounts for anyone else present at the Remote Point.
vocabulary.source: Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 5

institutions.summary: The police and the courts a s.138 case runs through in Haryana - the police grounded in the Haryana Police Act, 2007, the courts in the Constitution and the BNSS. The Punjab and Haryana High Court's rules of practice for the criminal courts are now in the corpus under State rules, as Volume III of its Rules and Orders.

police.summary: The Haryana Police, constituted under the Haryana Police Act, 2007. The force is organised into ranges, police districts and stations; the senior ranks are Indian Police Service (IPS) officers, the rest the Haryana Police Service. A s.138 case rarely involves the police (it is a complaint, not an FIR case).

story.summary: How a §138 cheque-bounce case runs in Kerala, from filing to disposal - built purely from the rules and Acts, with every step citing the provision that governs it. Click any citation to open the exact text. This is the de jure process the black-letter rules prescribe; the lived, local practice is a separate layer.

roles.who: The payee or the holder in due course of the dishonoured cheque. Only this person can set a §138 case going, by filing the complaint in their own name.

Where duly authorised and personally aware of the transaction, may file the complaint and depose on the complainant's behalf - a point the Supreme Court has settled for §138 cases. Stands in the payee's place, not as a separate party.
The drawer of the cheque, prosecuted for the dishonour. Where the drawer is a company, the company and every person who was in charge of and responsible to it.
Stands surety for the accused's release on bail, undertaking by bond to secure their appearance. The court tests the surety's sufficiency before accepting the bond.
The bank on which the cheque is drawn. Its return of the cheque unpaid is the event the offence turns on, and its return memo proves both the dishonour and the reason for it.
Gives evidence on the facts. In a §138 case the complainant's evidence may be led on affidavit, and an officer of the drawee bank often proves the dishonour. A witness is sworn before deposing.
The legal practitioner who appears for the complainant or the accused. The right to appear flows from enrolment under the Advocates Act.
Assists the advocate with filing, inspection of records and following the matter through the registry. A recognised court-precinct role rather than a statutory office.
roles.basis: Court-precinct and registry practice, governed by the High Court's rules rather than a provision of the substantive law.

roles.who: The Judicial Magistrate of the First Class who takes cognizance of the complaint, tries it summarily and passes judgment. In Kerala a §138 case may be assigned to the designated Special Court.
The court's senior ministerial officer who signs and issues the summons and other process 'by order of the Court'.
The clerk who attends the sitting: calls the cases, marks the exhibits, and keeps the court diary and the proceedings paper - the running record of each hearing.
Takes down the dictation of the depositions, orders and judgment. The depositions they record are headed and signed in the form the rules prescribe.

Interprets the evidence when a witness does not speak the court's language, which matters in Kerala where the court language is Malayalam. The interpreter is put on oath, and a police officer may not interpret the evidence.
The local police officer who executes warrants and serves the process the court issues, as part of the statutory functions of the police.

The court official (part of the Registry / ministerial establishment) who scrutinises a complaint and its documents for defects before it is numbered and placed for cognizance, noting objections or returning it for amendment.

informal.title: 'Scrutiny officer' is the functional name used on the ground; the rules assign scrutiny to 'the Registry' (E-Filing Rules r.17) and returns to the 'officer concerned' (CRP r.68).
informal.practice: Reported (Mehul, PUCAR; unverified): defects are sometimes not marked properly and files held so the advocate approaches the officer and may pay to move the file forward.

steps: A cheque-bounce case is a complaint case: the payee or holder in due course files a written complaint, and the Magistrate can take cognizance only on such a complaint (never on a police report).
It must be filed within one month of the cause of action - which arises when the drawer fails to pay within 15 days of the demand notice served after dishonour.
In Kerala the complaint is e-filed through the DCMS portal under the E-Filing Rules, and the court fee is paid on filing.

Before the complaint is numbered and placed for cognizance it is scrutinised for defects. On e-filing the Registry scrutinises the pleadings and documents and notes objections; a defective petition is not numbered and is returned to the party, pleader or officer concerned for amendment and representation.

On the ground this is done by an official commonly called the scrutiny officer. Reported (Mehul, PUCAR; unverified): defects are sometimes not marked properly and files held so the advocate approaches the officer and may pay to move the file forward. The scrutiny function is in the rules; the title and this practice are not.
The Magistrate examines the complainant (and any witnesses) on oath and, if satisfied there is ground to proceed, takes cognizance and issues process to the accused.
The summons is signed and issued by the court's ministerial officer 'by order of the Court', in the prescribed form.
Because the court language is Malayalam, process issued in Malayalam must carry an authorised English translation.
The summons is served in the manner the BNSS prescribes, and the NI Act's own mode of service also applies.
Service is effected through the police - the local Station House Officer serves the court's process. This is the only point at which the police enter a §138 case.
Where the e-filing regime permits, service may be by electronic means.

process.stage: 4 · If the accused does not appear
steps: The court escalates up the warrant ladder: a warrant issues, and on continued absconding, proclamation and attachment of property.
Kerala's rules carry the absconding-accused track; the police execute the warrant.
The case is tried summarily, and the complainant's evidence may be given on affidavit - the features that make §138 a fast-track offence.
A presumption operates in favour of the holder that the cheque was issued for a debt or liability, unless the accused rebuts it.
Kerala adds nothing procedural here - the summary-trial machinery is uniform central law.
On conviction the court may impose imprisonment up to two years and/or a fine up to twice the cheque amount, with compensation to the complainant.
The offence is compoundable: the parties may settle at any stage and the case is compounded, ending the prosecution.
The accused may appeal; the appellate court may require a deposit of a minimum of 20% of the fine/compensation as a condition of the appeal.
A revision lies to the High Court, whose own rules govern its criminal side.
A complaint may also be challenged by a quashing petition before the High Court.

vocabulary.gloss: The court officer who, 'by order of the Court', ordinarily signs and issues the summons to the accused and witnesses in a Kerala criminal court.
The prescribed words that must precede the ministerial officer's signature on a summons.
The court's running administrative record of a case (Administrative Form No. 10).
The sheet on which the day-to-day proceedings of a case are recorded (Judicial Form No. 61).
The officer in charge of a police station; in a s.138 case the person who executes the court's warrant and serves its process - the only point at which the police enter the case.
vocabulary.source: Kerala Police Act, §4 (functions of the police)
aka: officer in charge of the police station

vocabulary.gloss: The statutory duties of the Kerala police, including serving court process and executing warrants - a s.138 case is a complaint case, so the police act only on the court's process, never by investigation.
Court process issued in Malayalam must carry an authorised English translation - the point where the court-language rule bites on a summons or notice.
The working language of Kerala's subordinate courts; it shapes the summons, the demand-notice evidence, orders and the filing interface a s.138 case passes through.
The District Court Case Management System at filing.keralacourts.in through which a s.138 complaint is electronically filed in Kerala.
When the Kerala e-filing regime permits service by electronic means - narrower than informal WhatsApp/e-mail service, which the High Court has declined to sanction (Anoop Jacob).
Kollam's dedicated §138 court, running round-the-clock as India's first fully digital 'ON Court' - the concrete court the Kerala layer describes.
A Judicial Magistrate of the First Class court set up under the proviso to section 9(1) BNSS to try only cheque-bounce cases - Kerala's sits at Kollam.

The ad valorem fee to file a cheque complaint in Kerala - ₹250 up to a ₹10,000 cheque, otherwise 5% of the cheque amount capped at ₹3 lakh (Article 21, Court Fees Act; revised by the Finance Act 2025).
The clerk who attends the sitting - calls the cases, marks the exhibits, and keeps the court diary and the proceedings paper.
Takes down the dictation of the depositions, orders and judgment; the depositions are headed and signed as the rules prescribe.
Interprets the evidence when a witness does not speak the court's language, which in Kerala is Malayalam; put on oath, and a police officer may not interpret.
A person who stands surety for the accused's release on bail, undertaking by bond to secure their appearance; the court tests the surety's sufficiency.
Assists the advocate with filing, inspection of records and following the matter through the registry - a recognised court-precinct role rather than a statutory office.
vocabulary.source: Court-precinct and registry practice (not a statutory office)

vocabulary.gloss: How the national Oaths Act, 1969 requirement is run on the ground in Kerala: the Criminal Rules of Practice name the officer who administers the oath (Rule 50) and prescribe its form (Rule 51). A witness, interpreter or deponent is bound by it before giving evidence; one who objects to being sworn makes a solemn affirmation instead.

The document by which a party authorises an advocate to appear and act for them; until it is on record the advocate has no authority to represent the party. The Kerala Criminal Rules of Practice prescribe its form and attestation (Rule 32).

A witness's evidence as recorded in court and signed. The Kerala Criminal Rules of Practice prescribe how depositions are headed (Rule 56) and signed (Rule 57); in a summary §138 trial much of the evidence reaches the record as affidavits rather than long oral depositions.

The rules the High Court of Kerala made in 1982, under Article 227 of the Constitution, to govern how the criminal courts below it actually run - filing, the court diary, oaths, depositions, the vakalatnama, bail and so on. This site cites them as the source of most of the Kerala state-layer vocabulary.

The court official (part of the Registry / ministerial establishment) who scrutinises a complaint and its documents for defects before it is numbered and placed for cognizance. On e-filing the Registry scrutinises and notes objections (E-Filing Rules r.17); a defective petition is not numbered and is returned for amendment and representation (CRP r.68). 'Scrutiny officer' is the functional name used on the ground; the rules name 'the Registry' or the 'officer concerned', not this title.
vocabulary.source: E-Filing Rules, Kerala, r.17 (read with CRP r.68)

vocabulary.gloss: The court's administrative office - the ministerial establishment that receives filings, scrutinises them for defects, numbers and lists the case, keeps the records and issues process. A s.138 complaint is presented here before it reaches the Magistrate: the office checks the form and enclosures under the Criminal Rules of Practice (rule 27 on presentation of proceedings; rule 68 on returning defective petitions), and on e-filing the Electronic Filing Rules assign the same scrutiny to 'the Registry'. In the High Court the office is headed by the Registrar under the Rules of the High Court of Kerala, 1971.

The senior judicial officer who heads the High Court's registry - scrutiny, listing, custody of records and the exercise of delegated administrative and quasi-judicial powers. In a s.138 case the Registrar's office is where a criminal revision or a petition to quash the complaint is presented and scrutinised before it reaches the Bench. The Rules of the High Court of Kerala, 1971 set out the Registrar's powers and duties (Rule 15).
vocabulary.source: Rules of the High Court of Kerala, 1971, Rule 15

vocabulary.gloss: The District Police Chief - the officer who commands the whole police force of a district. A s.138 case rarely involves the police, but the Superintendent heads the district machinery that serves the court's process and executes its warrants. The rank sits in the Kerala Police ladder fixed by s.14 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011; the Police Act, 1861 (s.47) is the older source of the SP's district command.

The rank that is the Station House Officer of most police stations - the officer who, in an ordinary criminal case, registers the FIR and investigates, and who in a s.138 case serves the court's summons and executes its warrants. One of the Kerala Police ranks fixed by s.14 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011, with the station-house charge under s.5.

The Inspector of Police who heads a circle - a group of police stations - and is the Station House Officer of the larger stations, supervising the Sub-Inspectors under him. In a s.138 case he sits one level above the officer who serves the court's process. A Kerala Police rank fixed by s.14 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011.

The apex rank of the police and the head of the whole State force, in whom the administration, supervision and control of the entire Kerala Police is vested, subject to the Government. The role is remote from any single s.138 case but sits at the top of the machinery that serves the courts' process. The State Police Chief is designated under s.18 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011; the rank is the highest in the ladder fixed by s.14.

The head of a metropolitan Commissionerate - the unitary policing set up for larger cities such as Thiruvananthapuram and Kochi, where the Commissioner combines executive and certain magisterial powers. A s.138 case is tried by a court, not the police, but in a commissionerate city the Commissioner heads the force that serves the court's process. The commissionerate structure is provided for under s.15 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011.

The basic rank of the police - patrol, guard, beat duty and first response, and often the officer who physically carries and serves the court's process on the ground. Recruited directly through the Kerala PSC; the entrant must meet the eligibility in s.86 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011 and take the oath under s.87, and the rank is the first rung of the ladder fixed by s.14.

The oversight body that lays down broad policy for the police and insulates the force from illegitimate pressure. It has no role in any individual s.138 case but is part of the police-accountability structure the domain maps. Constituted under s.24 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011.

The body that inquires into serious complaints of misconduct against the police, such as custodial wrongdoing or abuse of authority. It does not touch the trial of a s.138 case but is the forum a citizen uses to hold errant officers to account. Constituted under s.110 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011.

institutions.summary: The two institutions a s.138 case runs through on the ground - the police and the courts - with their hierarchy, the people in each role, where each role comes from in law, and how a person enters it. Grounded in the Kerala Police Act, 2011 and the Police Act, 1861 for the police, and the Constitution, the BNSS and the Kerala court rules for the courts.

police.summary: One unified Kerala Police Force. The ranks, in ascending order, are fixed by s.14 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011; the senior ranks are Indian Police Service (IPS) officers, the rest the Kerala Police Service. A s.138 case rarely involves the police (it is a complaint, not an FIR case), but the force is part of the domain.

judiciary.summary: The court hierarchy a s.138 case moves through: the trial court is the Judicial Magistrate of the First Class; appeal lies to the Court of Session; revision and quashing to the High Court; and, by special leave, to the Supreme Court. Alongside the judges sits the court's ministerial establishment.

tiers.name: Supreme Court of India
tiers.who: The highest court. A s.138 matter reaches it only by special leave (art.136); its law binds every court in India (art.141).

tiers.name: High Court of Kerala
tiers.who: The State's highest court. In a s.138 case it hears criminal revisions and petitions to quash the complaint (s.482 CrPC / s.528 BNSS) and superintends the subordinate courts.

tiers.name: Court of Session (District & Sessions Court)
tiers.who: Headed by the District & Sessions Judge. It hears the first appeal from a s.138 conviction.

tiers.name: Chief Judicial Magistrate
tiers.who: Heads the magistracy of a district and has administrative control over the Judicial Magistrates.

tiers.name: Judicial Magistrate of the First Class
tiers.who: The trial court for a s.138 case: it takes cognizance of the complaint, tries it summarily, and on conviction sentences the accused.

roles.name: District & Sessions Judge
roles.who: Heads the district judiciary; hears sessions trials and s.138 appeals.
roles.entry: The Higher Judicial Service - direct recruitment of advocates with 7+ years' practice (art.233), or promotion from the subordinate judiciary.

roles.name: Judicial Magistrate (First Class)
roles.who: Tries the s.138 complaint - takes cognizance, records evidence, delivers judgment and sentence.
roles.entry: The Kerala Judicial Service - the Munsiff-Magistrate examination conducted by the Kerala PSC with the High Court (art.234).

roles.name: Sheristadar / Chief Ministerial Officer
roles.who: Head of the court's ministerial establishment; signs and issues the summons 'by order of the Court'.
roles.entry: Kerala ministerial (judicial) establishment, via the Kerala PSC and promotion.

roles.name: Bench Clerk
roles.who: Maintains the court's daily records, exhibits and order sheet during hearings.
roles.entry: Ministerial cadre, via the Kerala PSC.

roles.name: Registry / Scrutiny officer
roles.who: The court office that receives and scrutinises the filed complaint for defects before it goes for cognizance.
roles.entry: Ministerial cadre.

roles.name: Registrar (High Court)
roles.who: Heads the High Court registry - scrutiny, listing, custody of records.
roles.entry: A senior District Judge or a promoted officer of the establishment.

roles.name: Process server / Summons bailiff
roles.who: Serves the summons and warrants the court issues.
roles.entry: Ministerial cadre, via the Kerala PSC.

roles.name: Stenographer / Interpreter
roles.who: Records dictation and interprets a deposition into the court language (Malayalam in Kerala).
roles.entry: Ministerial cadre, via the Kerala PSC.

practice_notes.statement: In Kerala a scrutiny officer reviews litigant and advocate submissions and marks defects before the file is sent for taking cognizance. Reportedly the role is informal and not in the rules, and the officer often does not mark defects properly, holding files so the advocate approaches him and may make a payment to move the file forward.

claims.claim: a defect-scrutiny step happens before cognizance
the scrutiny role is informal and not in the rules
claims.note: Scrutiny is a formal function: the Registry scrutinises filings and notes objections under E-Filing Rules r.17, and CRP r.68 requires defective petitions to be returned for amendment and representation. Only the specific title 'scrutiny officer' and the file-holding-for-payment fall outside the rules.

practice_notes.statement: Filing assistants at the Panchkula lower-court window described how a s.138 ('NACT') case is filed. The advocate submits a physical file assembled in a fixed order - CIS proformas, index, memo of parties, the complaint (its 'prayer'), a Rs.10 court-fee ticket, an attested affidavit, the laminated cheque, an attested power of attorney and a copy per respondent. The assistant scrutinises it for completeness and attestation, enters it in the e-Courts CIS under Criminal then NACT, and the system issues a NACT filing number and a CNR number (HRPK...). The file is registered and carried the same day by a peon to the trial court, where the ahlmad takes over. They also described self-started practices: emailing a PDF copy to an office inbox kept on a desktop folder (unvalidated), laminating the cheque for safety (not mandatory), parking the jurisdictional police station under 'offence remarks' for case distribution, and using Google Translate as an OCR tool for long civil relief text (civil suits, not NACT). For e-filings, only the computer room can release a case into their queue, so they phone it repeatedly; advocates often leave non-mandatory fields (FIR number, police station) blank, which the assistants then fill in.

claims.claim: a s.138 complaint is received and scrutinised for defects at the filing window before it reaches the trial court
claims.method: firsthand account, consistent with the national filing and cognizance scheme

claims.claim: the limitation to file a s.138 complaint is '45 days'
claims.note: The statute gives one month from the cause of action to file (NI §142(1)(b)); the cause of action arises 15 days after the demand notice (§138 proviso). '45 days' looks like a practical rule of thumb combining the 15-day notice window with the one-month filing period, not a statutory 45-day limit. Safe as a conservative check, but it should be computed from the actual dates in each case.

claims.claim: a NACT (s.138) filing needs an FIR number and a jurisdictional police station
claims.note: A s.138 case is a complaint offence with no FIR and no police investigation, so the FIR field in the shared CIS criminal template does not apply to it. The 'police station' the assistants record is used only to distribute cases (by the bank where the cheque was presented), not for any investigation.

claims.claim: a PDF copy of each file is emailed to an office inbox and kept on the desktop as a record
claims.note: A recently self-started, informal practice - not required by any rule and not validated; the copy sits in a local desktop folder. Recorded as practice, not as an official record.

claims.claim: the cheque is laminated at filing
claims.note: An informal safety habit, explicitly not mandatory; its absence is not a ground to reject the file.

claims.claim: e-filed cases can only be released into the filing branch's queue by the computer room, and advocates skip non-mandatory fields
claims.note: An access-control and data-quality gap described firsthand: the branch has no direct release permission (10 to 15 calls a day), and non-mandatory fields left blank in e-filing are re-entered by the assistants. A direct signal for portal design - make the paper-mandatory fields mandatory online.

cases.name: Rangappa v. Sri Mohan
cases.holding: The s.139 presumption extends to the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability; it places a reverse onus on the accused, rebuttable on the preponderance of probabilities.

cases.name: Kumar Exports v. Sharma Carpets
cases.holding: Explains how the ss.118 and 139 presumptions operate and the evidentiary standard for rebutting them.

cases.name: Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa
cases.holding: Consolidated the principles on the s.139 presumption and the accused's 'probable defence' standard of rebuttal.

cases.name: Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar
cases.holding: A signed but blank/incomplete cheque voluntarily handed over still attracts the s.139 presumption, even if it was filled in by another person.

cases.name: Kalamani Tex v. P. Balasubramanian
cases.holding: Reaffirmed that the presumption is rebuttable only by a probable defence, not by bare denial.

cases.name: Oriental Bank of Commerce v. Prabodh Kumar Tewari
cases.holding: The s.139 presumption is rebuttable; the accused need only raise a probable defence on preponderance of probabilities.

cases.name: Rajesh Jain v. Ajay Singh
cases.holding: Restated in detail the burden-shifting sequence between complainant and accused under ss.118/139.

cases.name: Sunil Todi v. State of Gujarat
cases.holding: 'Debt or other liability' is read broadly; a cheque given for a liability that crystallises later can attract s.138.

cases.name: Dashrathbhai Trikambhai Patel v. Hitesh Mahendrabhai Patel
cases.holding: Part-payments made after issuance but before encashment must be endorsed (s.56); dishonour of the unendorsed cheque does not attract s.138 unless the sum is a legally enforceable debt at maturity.

cases.name: Sampelly Satyanarayana Rao v. Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency
cases.holding: Cheques issued towards future instalments/security can still represent a subsisting debt or liability for s.138.

cases.name: K. Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan
cases.holding: Identified the five component acts making up the cause of action under s.138 (drawing, presentment, dishonour, notice, failure to pay).
cases.note: The jurisdictional 'any of five places' aspect was later narrowed by Dashrath Rupsingh and then reset by the 2015 amendment.

cases.name: C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed
cases.holding: Deemed service of the s.138 demand notice under s.27 General Clauses Act — a notice returned 'unclaimed' is deemed served; the drawer may still avoid liability by paying within 15 days of receiving the summons.

cases.name: MSR Leathers v. S. Palaniappan
cases.holding: A payee may present the cheque repeatedly and issue successive notices; a prosecution can be based on any subsequent dishonour.

cases.name: Sadanandan Bhadran v. Madhavan Sunil Kumar
cases.holding: Had held that only one cause of action arises per cheque.

cases.name: Yogendra Pratap Singh v. Savitri Pandey
cases.holding: No cognizance can be taken before the 15-day notice period expires; a complaint filed prematurely is not maintainable.

cases.name: Gajanand Burange v. Laxmi Chand Goyal
cases.holding: A complaint filed before expiry of the 15-day notice period is non-maintainable; a fresh complaint may be filed within the s.142(b) window with delay condoned for sufficient cause.

cases.name: Dashrath Rupsingh Rathod v. State of Maharashtra
cases.holding: Fixed territorial jurisdiction at the place where the drawee bank (on which the cheque was drawn) is located.

relations.note: jurisdiction reset to payee's bank branch (s.142(2)/s.142A)

cases.name: Bridgestone India Pvt Ltd v. Inderpal Singh
cases.holding: Upheld the 2015 amendment; jurisdiction lies where the payee's/holder's bank branch is situated, and s.142A validates transfer of pending cases.

cases.name: A.C. Narayanan v. State of Maharashtra
cases.holding: A power-of-attorney holder can file the complaint and depose, provided he has personal knowledge of the transaction and is duly authorised.

cases.name: TRL Krosaki Refractories Ltd v. SMS Asia Pvt Ltd
cases.holding: A company's complaint may be filed and deposed to by an authorised employee; authorisation is presumed unless specifically disputed.

cases.name: S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Neeta Bhalla
cases.holding: A complaint must specifically aver that the director was in charge of, and responsible to the company for, the conduct of its business at the relevant time.

cases.name: National Small Industries Corp Ltd v. Harmeet Singh Paintal
cases.holding: Reiterated the specific-averment requirement; the position of a managing director/signatory differs from that of an ordinary director.

cases.name: Aneeta Hada v. Godfather Travels & Tours Pvt Ltd
cases.holding: For vicarious liability under s.141 the company must be arraigned as an accused; a director cannot be convicted without the company being prosecuted.

cases.name: Gunmala Sales Pvt Ltd v. Anu Mehta
cases.holding: Laid down guidelines on when a High Court may quash s.141 proceedings against a director.

cases.name: Sunita Palita v. Panchami Stone Quarry
cases.holding: Non-executive and independent directors cannot be roped in without specific averments and material showing their role in the conduct of business.

cases.name: S.P. Mani & Mohan Dairy v. Snehalatha Elangovan
cases.holding: A partner's vicarious liability requires an averment/showing that the partner was in charge of and responsible for the firm's business at the relevant time.

cases.name: Dilip Hariramani v. Bank of Baroda
cases.holding: The firm/company must itself be prosecuted; a partner cannot be convicted merely as a signatory or guarantor without the firm being an accused.

cases.name: Siby Thomas v. M/s Somany Ceramics Ltd
cases.holding: A bare reproduction of the statutory words is not enough; the complaint must contain a clear averment of the accused's role in the conduct of business.

cases.name: Mandvi Cooperative Bank Ltd v. Nimesh B. Thakore
cases.holding: Explains the scope of s.145 (evidence on affidavit); the accused cannot insist on the complainant being examined-in-chief in court as of right.

cases.name: Indian Bank Association v. Union of India
cases.holding: Issued omnibus directions for speedy disposal of s.138 cases (form and service of summons, one-day evidence, use of technology).

cases.name: Meters and Instruments Pvt Ltd v. Kanchan Mehta
cases.holding: Treated the offence as primarily compensatory and suggested a court could close proceedings on payment even without the complainant's consent.

relations.note: suo-motu closure / s.258 point held not good law

cases.name: In re Expeditious Trial of Cases under Section 138 of NI Act, 1881
cases.holding: Constitution Bench: clarified that s.258 CrPC closure is not available in s.138 complaint cases (disapproving Meters & Instruments on that point), addressed service of summons and a single inquiry for multiple complaints, and directed High Courts to frame rules for expeditious trial.

relations.note: on the s.258 suo-motu closure point only

cases.name: Damodar S. Prabhu v. Sayed Babalal H
cases.holding: Laid down graded-cost guidelines to encourage early compounding of s.138 offences, invoking Article 142.

cases.name: JIK Industries Ltd v. Amarlal V. Jumani
cases.holding: Compounding under s.147 read with s.320 CrPC ordinarily requires the consent of the complainant.

cases.name: Raj Reddy Kallem v. State of Haryana
cases.holding: The Supreme Court may quash a s.138 conviction on the accused compensating the complainant even without the complainant's consent, using Article 142 — distinguishing 'quashing' from statutory 'compounding'.

cases.name: New Win Export v. A. Subramaniam
cases.holding: Reiterated that dishonour is a regulatory offence and that courts should encourage compounding.

cases.name: G.J. Raja v. Tejraj Surana
cases.holding: Section 143A (interim compensation up to 20%) is prospective only and does not apply to offences committed before its insertion.

cases.name: Surinder Singh Deswal v. Virender Gandhi
cases.holding: Section 148 (deposit of minimum 20% to maintain an appeal) applies to appeals even where the cheque pre-dates the amendment; the appellate 'may' is ordinarily to be read as 'shall'.

cases.name: Jamboo Bhandari v. M.P. State Industrial Development Corp Ltd
cases.holding: The s.148 deposit is not automatic; the appellate court must apply its mind and record reasons, and may waive the deposit in appropriate/exceptional cases.

cases.name: Kaushalya Devi Massand v. Roopkishore Khore
cases.holding: The s.138 offence is quasi-criminal and primarily compensatory in character.

cases.name: R. Vijayan v. Baby
cases.holding: Compensation should ordinarily be awarded in s.138 cases, generally keyed to the cheque amount with interest and costs.

cases.name: Suganthi Suresh Kumar v. Jagdeeshan
cases.holding: Courts should not lightly reduce sentence or compensation below the norm in cheque-dishonour cases.

cases.name: Sanjabij Tari v. State (and connected matters)
cases.holding: Directs courts to consider the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 in appropriate s.138 cases when sentencing.
